adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal-priority default, Elytron, and FIPS providers are selected by classpath iteration order, so a FIPS deployment can silently run a non-FIPS provider instead of failing closed

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — An early or failed AuthzClient creation can permanently install the incomplete fallback in the process-wide singleton and cascade UnsupportedOperationException failures into unrelated Keycloak crypto users

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows CryptoIntegration.init() is called in AuthzClient.create() at line 95. Looking at CryptoIntegration.java, the detectProvider() method uses ServiceLoader to find CryptoProvider implementations and selects the one with highest order(). The AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order() returning 100, while DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. This means when multiple providers are available, the AuthzClientCryptoProvider (with its many UnsupportedOperationException methods) would NOT be selected over the full implementations. However, if AuthzClient is used in isolation (without the full crypto providers on classpath), the incomplete AuthzClientCryptoProvider gets installed as a process-wide singleton. If later code in the same process expects full crypto functionality, it would fail. The finding correctly identifies that early initialization with the limited provider could affect other Keycloak crypto users in the same process.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — The verifier conversion ignores bytes beyond signLength, so a valid ECDSA signature with attacker-appended garbage is accepted as the same signature

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that the asn1derToConcatenatedRS method ignores bytes beyond signLength, allowing attacker-appended garbage. However, looking at the code in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java lines 109-130, the method reads the ASN1 sequence from derEncodedSignatureValue, extracts exactly two integers (r and s), and converts them to fixed-length byte arrays. The ASN1Decoder.readSequence() method properly parses the DER structure and would fail or ignore trailing garbage at the ASN1 parsing level, not at the signature verification level. The signature verification itself happens elsewhere (in the JCA Signature class), not in this conversion method. This method only converts between signature formats. Any trailing garbage in the input would either cause ASN1 parsing to fail or be ignored during format conversion, but the actual cryptographic verification happens separately.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:153 — Oversized or negative DER integers are silently truncated or padded instead of rejected, allowing hostile noncanonical inputs to alias raw signatures

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that oversized or negative DER integers are 'silently truncated or padded instead of rejected'. Looking at the integerToBytes method at line 153, it handles size mismatches by either truncating (when bytes.length > qLength) or padding (when bytes.length < qLength). This is actually the correct behavior for ECDSA signature conversion - the method is converting BigInteger representations to fixed-length byte arrays for concatenated RS format. The truncation removes leading zeros (or sign extension bytes), and padding adds leading zeros. This is standard practice for ECDSA signature format conversion, not a security vulnerability. The code correctly handles the conversion between ASN.1 DER format and concatenated RS format.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:57 — Sequence parsing accepts a child that overruns the declared sequence length and ignores bytes trailing the sequence rather than rejecting malformed DER

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the readSequence() method in ASN1Decoder.java lines 49-60, the code reads the sequence length, then iterates reading children while length > 0, subtracting each child's byte length. However, if a child's declared length exceeds the remaining sequence length, the code will still read it (potentially reading beyond the sequence boundary). Additionally, after the while loop completes, there's no validation that all bytes in the input were consumed - trailing bytes after the sequence would be silently ignored. This is a valid DER parsing strictness issue that could accept malformed input.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — The test only compares two converter outputs and never verifies the converted signature, so symmetric corruption and acceptance of trailing signature bytes pass silently

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a limitation in the test. Looking at the test code in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java, the test method creates a signature, converts it from ASN1DER to concatenated RS format, then back to ASN1DER, then back to concatenated RS again, and only asserts that rsConcat equals rsConcat2. The test never verifies the signature against the original data using the public key, which means it only tests round-trip consistency of the conversion, not correctness. This is a valid concern about test coverage for newly added cryptographic code - the test could pass even if the conversion produces invalid signatures, as long as the conversion is symmetric.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal provider orders now select a classpath-order-dependent winner instead of rejecting the ambiguous configuration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a design change in the diff. Looking at lines 54-67 of CryptoIntegration.java, the old code threw an exception when multiple providers were found, while the new code sorts by order() (reversed) and picks the first one. If two providers have the same order() value, the selection becomes dependent on ServiceLoader iteration order (which is classpath-dependent). This is a valid architectural concern - the code no longer fails-fast on ambiguous configurations. However, this appears to be intentional design (to allow the new AuthzClientCryptoProvider with order=100 to coexist with existing providers at order=200), so it's a design decision rather than a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:58 — The service-registered CryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException from most methods and therefore does not satisfy the interface contract for consumers.

adjudication.rationale: The AuthzClientCryptoProvider is intentionally designed as a minimal crypto provider for the authz-client module. It implements only the methods needed for that specific use case (getEcdsaCryptoProvider, getKeyStore, getBouncyCastleProvider) and throws UnsupportedOperationException for methods that are not needed. This is a valid design pattern - the provider has order=100 (lower priority than the full providers at order=200), so it will only be used when no other provider is available. The interface contract doesn't require all methods to be implemented - it's acceptable to throw UnsupportedOperationException for unused functionality. The test file shows the provider works correctly for its intended purpose (ECDSA operations).

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:61 — getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider rather than the Bouncy Castle provider promised by the interface.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:63 — getBouncyCastleProvider returns the provider for the JVM default keystore instead of a BouncyCastle provider.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider() which returns the JVM's default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider. Looking at the diff, this is intentional - the AuthzClientCryptoProvider is a minimal crypto provider for the authz-client that doesn't require BouncyCastle. The method name is misleading but the implementation appears deliberate for this lightweight provider. This is a valid architectural/naming concern but not a bug since the provider is designed to work without BouncyCastle.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — Client construction now fixes a process-wide crypto singleton from one classloader, coupling every later consumer to whichever factory call initializes it first

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that CryptoIntegration.init() is called in AuthzClient.create() with a specific classloader, and CryptoIntegration uses a static singleton pattern (as seen in the diff showing 'private static CryptoProvider cryptoProvider'). This means the first call to AuthzClient.create() will lock in the crypto provider for the entire process. This is a legitimate architectural concern about the coupling introduced by this change - different consumers using different classloaders could have unexpected behavior depending on initialization order. However, this appears to be intentional design (the detectProvider method was modified to handle multiple providers via ordering), so it's a scope/architecture concern rather than a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:58 — Implementing the server-wide CryptoProvider for two client operations leaves most capabilities as runtime stubs, so future common callers compile against methods this provider cannot support

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider but throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods (getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getKeyFactory, getSignature, etc.). This is a legitimate architectural concern - the class implements a broad interface but only supports a narrow subset of operations (getEcdsaCryptoProvider, getKeyStore, getBouncyCastleProvider). While this is intentional for the authz-client use case (order=100 vs 200 for full providers), it creates a fragile situation where code depending on CryptoProvider could fail at runtime if this provider is selected. The finding is grounded in the actual diff showing the stub implementations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Provider precedence relies on duplicated magic integers and equal priorities silently fall back to ServiceLoader order, creating implicit cross-module coupling when providers are added

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new ordering mechanism uses hardcoded integers (100 for AuthzClientCryptoProvider, 200 for others) and that equal priorities would fall back to ServiceLoader order. This is visible in the diff: AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100, while DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. The sorting in CryptoIntegration.java uses Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed() which would have undefined behavior for equal values. This is a legitimate architectural concern about implicit coupling, though it's not a bug since the current values are distinct.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:43 — Making order abstract causes existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations to throw AbstractMethodError during provider initialization after upgrade

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that CryptoProvider interface adds a new method `int order()` at line 43. This is a new abstract method in an interface. Any existing third-party implementations of CryptoProvider that were compiled against the old interface version will not have this method implemented. When the JVM tries to call `order()` on such implementations (as shown in CryptoIntegration.java line 57 where `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` is called), it will throw AbstractMethodError. This is a real binary compatibility issue for existing implementations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Providers that share the same order are selected by class-loader discovery order, so an ambiguous default/FIPS/Elytron classpath silently initializes an arbitrary crypto mode

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that when multiple CryptoProviders have the same order value (e.g., DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all have order() returning 200), the selection depends on ServiceLoader discovery order, which is non-deterministic. The diff shows the code sorts by order in reverse (line 57: `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`) and takes the first one. While this is a valid design concern about ambiguous provider selection when orders are equal, it's not strictly a bug since the system will still function - it's more of an architectural/design concern that could lead to unexpected behavior in certain classpath configurations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:73 — A zero-length DER INTEGER throws unchecked NumberFormatException instead of the declared IOException, allowing a malformed ECDSA signature to escape the normal verification failure path

adjudication.rationale: Looking at ASN1Decoder.java line 73, the readInteger() method reads bytes via `read(length)` and then creates a BigInteger with `new BigInteger(bytes)`. The finding claims a zero-length INTEGER would throw NumberFormatException, but examining the code: if length is 0, `read(0)` returns an empty byte array, and `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` does throw NumberFormatException. However, this is not a bug introduced by this diff - it's actually correct behavior for malformed ASN.1 data. A zero-length INTEGER is invalid per DER encoding rules, so throwing an exception (even if it's NumberFormatException instead of IOException) is appropriate. The signature verification would still fail. Additionally, the method signature declares `throws IOException`, and the caller would need to handle any exception anyway. This is a minor implementation detail, not a real defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:63 — getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider instead of Bouncy Castle, so cryptographic operations can run outside the intended provider and FIPS boundary

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider() which returns the default keystore provider, not Bouncy Castle. However, looking at the context, this is a minimal crypto provider for the authz-client that explicitly throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods. The class is designed as a lightweight fallback provider (order=100, lower than the real providers at order=200) that only implements the bare minimum needed for ECDSA signature conversion. The getBouncyCastleProvider() implementation is intentionally returning a non-BC provider because this provider is meant for environments without BC. This is a design decision, not a bug, but it's a valid architectural concern worth discussing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:47 — Directly constructing the provider bypasses AuthzClient.create and ServiceLoader, so the new registration and initialization path has no effective test coverage.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java directly instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider with 'new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()' rather than going through AuthzClient.create() which calls CryptoIntegration.init(). This means the ServiceLoader registration path (via META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider) and the CryptoIntegration.init() initialization added in AuthzClient.create() are not exercised by this test. The test only verifies the ECDSA conversion logic works, not that the provider is properly registered and loaded. This is a valid observation about incomplete test coverage for the new initialization path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — The new multiple-provider priority selection behavior is untested, including higher-order selection and equal-order handling.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new priority-based provider selection logic in CryptoIntegration.java (lines 56-68) that sorts providers by order() and selects the highest. While there is a test file added (ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java), it only tests ECDSA algorithm functionality, not the provider selection mechanism itself. The finding correctly identifies that the new multi-provider priority selection behavior (including what happens with equal orders, edge cases with single provider, etc.) lacks dedicated unit tests. This is a legitimate concern for newly added nontrivial logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — Reusing one uninitialized default EC key for every algorithm means ES384 and ES512 do not exercise their required 48-byte and 66-byte coordinate widths.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test uses a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() without specifying curve parameters. This generates a default curve (typically P-256/secp256r1) for all three test methods (ES256, ES384, ES512). ES384 requires P-384 (48-byte coordinates) and ES512 requires P-521 (66-byte coordinates). While the ASN1 encoding/decoding logic being tested may still work with mismatched key sizes (since it uses algorithm.getSignatureLength() for the expected lengths), the test doesn't properly exercise the full byte-width handling for ES384 and ES512. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added cryptographic code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:53 — Only valid JCA-produced DER is tested, leaving malformed tags, truncated or inconsistent lengths, extra sequence elements, and oversized integers unverified in the new custom decoder.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test ECDSAAlgorithmTest only tests the round-trip conversion using valid JCA-produced DER signatures. The test at line 53 calls asn1derToConcatenatedRS with a valid signature from Java's Signature class, then converts back and forth. The new ASN1Decoder class (lines 1-203 in the new file) contains complex parsing logic for tags, lengths, and sequences that could fail on malformed input, but no tests verify error handling for invalid inputs like malformed tags, truncated data, extra sequence elements, or oversized integers. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for newly added nontrivial parsing logic.
